utterance:
Thanks Daniel. Here's what I found and what I think is going on.

The good news: your examination is reassuring. There are no signs of anything serious — no fever, no nerve problems (your strength, reflexes and sensation are all normal), and no warning signs in your back itself. What I found is tenderness and muscle spasm on the left side of your lower back, with pain when you bend — that fits with a mechanical back strain from lifting that pot plant on Saturday. The pain spreading into your left buttock is very common with this and doesn't mean a trapped nerve, because it doesn't go down your leg and your leg neurology is completely normal.

About the MRI: I understand you'd like one, and I want to explain why I don't think it's needed right now. Scans like MRI are really good at showing discs and nerves, but in the first few weeks of a simple back strain, they rarely change what we do — most people's scans show things that are normal for their age and don't match the pain. Guidelines recommend imaging only when there are red flags (which you don't have), when pain lasts more than about 6 weeks, or when there are nerve symptoms like weakness or numbness. An MRI now would likely show something incidental and could lead you down a path of worry or treatment you don't need. The best evidence is that these strains settle with time and keeping moving.

So my plan:
1. Pain relief: I've prescribed ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day with food for 5 days, plus paracetamol 1 gram (two tablets) every 6 hours as needed. Take them regularly for the next few days rather than waiting for the pain to be bad. (I've noted your tramadol allergy — we won't use that.)
2. Stay active: the single most important thing is to avoid bed rest. Keep doing gentle movement — short walks around the house, change position regularly, and gradually return to normal activity and work as the pain allows. Lying on the couch all day actually slows recovery. Heat packs are fine to keep using.
3. Physio: if it's not improving over the next 1–2 weeks, a few sessions with a physiotherapist can help with exercises and getting you back to full activity.

Safety-netting — please seek urgent care or call an ambulance, or get back to me urgently, if you develop: new weakness, numbness or tingling in your legs; any problem passing urine or opening your bowels, or numbness in your saddle/groin area; fever or feeling unwell; or pain that is rapidly getting much worse.

If things aren't clearly improving after about 6 weeks, or you develop leg symptoms, come back and we can reconsider imaging then. Does that all make sense, and do you have any questions?
reply: Honestly? I've been reading about slipped discs and people needing surgery.

awards.label: What he is worried the pain might be

utterance:
That's a really common worry, and it's good you've raised it — let me put your mind at ease.

A 'slipped disc' (a disc pressing on a nerve) usually causes pain that travels down the leg, often below the knee, with numbness, tingling or weakness in the leg or foot. Your examination shows none of that — your straight leg raise test was normal, your strength, reflexes and sensation are all perfect. Your pain staying in the back and buttock, worse with bending and movement, is the classic picture of a muscle and ligament strain, not a disc problem.

Even when a disc is involved, the good news is that the body often reabsorbs it over weeks to months, and most people recover fully with time, activity and pain relief — only a small minority ever need surgery, and surgery is reserved for people with persistent nerve compression causing weakness or bladder/bowel problems. Scanning everyone early doesn't improve outcomes; it just finds things that don't need treating.

So the plan stays the same: stay active, use the pain relief regularly, and give it time. The safety-netting I mentioned covers the rare situations where we would act quickly. Any other questions, or anything else worrying you?
reply: That makes sense, and I am glad my legs are normal. I will start the ibuprofen and try to get up and move around more instead of staying on the couch.

awards.label: Defensible diagnosis: Mechanical low back pain
Can't-miss diagnosis considered: Cauda equina syndrome
